Sign off: the EM check must pass at the maximum specified junction temperature (typically 125C) for the product lifetime (typically 10 years for consumer, 15-20 years for automotive). Apply appropriate acceleration factors from the EM model.

steps.description: Analyze noise injection into the substrate from digital switching and assess its impact on sensitive analog circuits sharing the die.

inputs.name: die-floorplan
inputs.desc: Block placement with analog and digital locations

inputs.name: switching-activity
inputs.desc: Digital switching current waveforms

outputs.name: substrate-noise-map
outputs.desc: Noise voltage at each analog block location from digital switching

outputs.name: mitigation-recommendations
outputs.desc: Guard ring, spacing, and biasing changes to reduce coupling below threshold

process: Digital circuits inject noise into the substrate through two mechanisms: (1) capacitive coupling from switching drains through the drain-substrate junction capacitance, (2) resistive coupling through substrate contacts carrying bounce current from simultaneous switching output (SSO).

Model the substrate as a 3D resistive network. Substrate resistivity in bulk CMOS is typically 10-20 Ohm*cm for p-type. For high-resistivity substrates (used in RF), 1000+ Ohm*cm. Higher resistivity provides better isolation at DC but worse at high frequency (less capacitive bypassing).

Calculate the coupling: noise voltage at the analog location = substrate noise current * mutual impedance between digital injector and analog sensor. The mutual impedance decreases with distance approximately as 1/r for a point source in a conductive half-plane.

Sensitive nodes in analog circuits: the bulk terminal of NMOS transistors sitting in the p-substrate. Substrate voltage variation modulates Vt through the body effect: delta_Vt = gamma * delta_Vsb / (2*sqrt(2*phi_F + Vsb)), where gamma is the body effect coefficient (typically 0.3-0.5 V^0.5).

Mitigation: (1) Deep n-well under sensitive analog NMOS (isolates from substrate noise by 20-40 dB), (2) Dense substrate contacts around analog blocks (reduce local substrate resistance), (3) Increase physical separation (each doubling of distance reduces coupling by approximately 6 dB), (4) Separate analog and digital VSS at the die level (connect at package only).

Simulate with a substrate extraction tool: extract the substrate RC network between identified aggressor and victim locations. Inject the digital switching current waveform and measure the voltage at analog nodes. Compare to the analog sensitivity threshold (e.g., 1 mV for a 10-bit ADC with 1V reference).

description: Execute the digital physical design flow from synthesis through placement, clock tree synthesis, routing, and sign-off extraction and timing analysis for an ASIC.

steps.description: Translate RTL timing requirements into synthesis constraints (SDC) and configure the synthesis tool for the target PPA (performance, power, area).

inputs.name: rtl-design
inputs.desc: Verified RTL code (Verilog/VHDL)

inputs.name: timing-requirements
inputs.desc: Clock frequency, I/O timing, multicycle paths, false paths

inputs.name: target-library
inputs.desc: Standard cell library for the target process and voltage corner

outputs.name: synthesis-constraints-sdc
outputs.desc: SDC file with clocks, I/O delays, exceptions, and design rule constraints

outputs.name: synthesized-netlist
outputs.desc: Gate-level netlist meeting timing constraints

process: Define clocks in SDC: create_clock with period, waveform edges, and uncertainty. Clock uncertainty at synthesis should include estimated post-layout skew plus jitter. Typical pre-layout uncertainty: 200-500 ps depending on clock frequency and methodology.

Set input and output delays: set_input_delay and set_output_delay define when data arrives at input ports and when it must be stable at output ports relative to the clock. These come from the interface timing budget (board-level or chip-to-chip).

Define timing exceptions: set_false_path for paths that never propagate functionally (e.g., between asynchronous clock domains, test-only paths). set_multicycle_path for paths allowed more than one clock cycle (gray-code logic, pipelined buses with valid signals).

Set area and power constraints: set_max_area as a target (synthesis will optimize to meet timing first, then area). Power intent through UPF: define power domains, isolation cells, level shifters, retention registers if the design has multiple power states.

Run synthesis: the tool maps RTL to standard cells, optimizes for timing (meet setup at worst corner), applies design rule fixes (max fanout, max transition, max capacitance). Use multi-corner multi-mode (MCMM): optimize simultaneously for setup at slow corner and hold at fast corner.

Review synthesis results: check timing slack at all corners (positive slack means timing met), area utilization (target 70-80% for routability), power estimate (toggle-rate-based), and cell count. If timing is negative, review the critical path and consider micro-architectural changes.

steps.description: Create the physical floorplan with macro placement, blockage definition, I/O placement, and power ring/stripe design to meet IR drop and routability targets.

inputs.name: synthesized-netlist
inputs.desc: Gate-level netlist with area and pin information

inputs.name: die-size-target
inputs.desc: Target die dimensions and I/O ring configuration

outputs.name: floorplan
outputs.desc: Placed macros, I/O pads, and blockage definitions

outputs.name: power-plan
outputs.desc: Power rings and stripes with estimated IR drop

process: Place hard macros (SRAMs, analog blocks, PLLs): locate close to their I/O connections to minimize wire length. Maintain minimum spacing between macros for routing channels. Add placement and routing blockages around macros to prevent standard cells from being placed too close (cell-to-macro spacing rule).

Create power rings around the core and around each macro. Ring width is set by the EM current limit and the current draw of the enclosed region. Typical top-metal ring width: 5-20 um. Add power stripes across the core connecting the rings, spaced to meet the IR drop target.

Via down from the power stripes to the standard cell power rails (typically on metal-1). Each via stack must be sized to carry the local current demand. Use via arrays, not single vias, for power connections.

Define placement regions: group related logic (clock domain, pipeline stage, data-path slice) into soft regions to guide placement for better timing and lower wire length. Do not over-constrain: leave the placer freedom to optimize globally.

Run trial placement (coarse): check congestion (regions where routing demand exceeds available tracks), timing (are macro placements creating long wire detours?), and power grid IR drop with estimated switching activity. Iterate the floorplan to resolve congestion hot spots.

Finalize I/O pad placement: pads are typically placed on a fixed pitch on the die perimeter. Assign signal pins to minimize wirelength to their internal logic. Place power and ground pads at regular intervals (every 5-10 signal pads) to maintain low supply impedance.

steps.description: Build the clock distribution network to meet skew, insertion delay, and OCV derating targets while minimizing clock power.

inputs.name: floorplan
inputs.desc: Placed design with clock source and sink locations

inputs.name: timing-requirements
inputs.desc: Clock uncertainty budget, skew target, and insertion delay limit

outputs.name: clock-tree
outputs.desc: Synthesized clock tree with buffer placement and routing

outputs.name: clock-tree-report
outputs.desc: Skew, insertion delay, transition time, and power of the clock network

process: Define CTS constraints: target skew (typically 50-200 ps), maximum insertion delay (to control clock latency for I/O timing), maximum transition time at sinks (fast transitions reduce short-circuit power and improve hold margin), and buffer cell list (which clock buffer cells the tool may use).

The CTS algorithm: starting from the clock source, recursively partition the clock sinks into balanced groups. Insert buffers to drive each group, balancing the capacitive load and wire delay at each level. The result is a balanced tree with equalized path lengths.

CTS with OCV (on-chip variation) derating: at each tree level, the delay can vary by +/- the OCV factor (typically 5-10%). To ensure hold timing, the early path must not arrive too early: this constrains the minimum skew between any two sinks. Apply CRPR (clock reconvergence pessimism removal) to avoid double-counting variation on shared tree segments.

For useful skew: intentionally adding skew can help timing. If path A to B has negative slack but the clock to B is late relative to A, adding positive skew (delivering the clock earlier to the launching flip-flop or later to the capturing flip-flop) recovers slack. CTS tools support useful-skew optimization.

Clock gating: insert clock gate cells (ICG) before the tree fans out to blocks that can be disabled. The ICG cell AND-gates the clock with an enable signal, stopping the clock to idle blocks. This reduces dynamic power by 20-50% in typical designs. Place ICGs close to the block they gate to maximize power savings.

Post-CTS timing: run timing analysis with the actual clock tree delays (not the estimated uncertainty). Setup and hold timing should both pass. If hold violations exist, insert delay buffers on the data path (hold fixing). Verify that clock tree power is within budget (clock typically consumes 30-50% of dynamic power).

steps.description: Optimize standard cell placement for timing and congestion, then route the design, resolving DRC violations and timing degradation from routing parasitics.

inputs.name: clock-tree
inputs.desc: Design with CTS completed

inputs.name: floorplan
inputs.desc: Macro placement and power plan

outputs.name: routed-design
outputs.desc: Fully routed layout passing DRC

outputs.name: routing-report
outputs.desc: Wire length, via count, congestion, and timing after routing

process: Placement optimization: the placer positions standard cells to minimize wirelength (half-perimeter bounding box), meet timing (place connected cells closer together on critical paths), and reduce congestion (spread cells in dense regions). Run incremental placement after CTS to refine.

Timing-driven placement: cells on critical paths are pulled together. Cells with high fanout are placed centrally relative to their loads. The placer uses estimated wire delays (based on wire length and layer assignment) to optimize timing before routing.

Global routing: assigns each net to routing channels (gcells) across the chip without specifying exact tracks. This determines the routing congestion map. If any gcell is over-capacity (more nets than available tracks), the placer must spread cells or the router will detour wires (adding delay).

Detailed routing: assigns each wire to a specific metal track and layer, inserts vias for layer transitions, and resolves DRC violations (minimum spacing, minimum width, via enclosure). The router optimizes for minimum wirelength and via count while meeting DRC.

Post-route optimization: after initial routing, some timing paths degrade due to routing detours or coupling capacitance. Run post-route optimization: the tool can upsize drivers, insert buffers, and reroute critical nets on preferred (less congested, lower-resistance) layers.

DRC cleanup: after routing, run a full DRC check. Common violations: metal spacing (fix by jog or reroute), via enclosure (fix by shifting via placement), antenna ratio (fix by adding jumper to higher metal or antenna diode). Iterate until zero DRC violations.

steps.description: Extract parasitic RC from the routed layout, run multi-corner static timing analysis for signoff, and verify timing closure with OCV and CRPR.

inputs.name: routed-design
inputs.desc: DRC-clean routed layout

inputs.name: synthesis-constraints-sdc
inputs.desc: Timing constraints

outputs.name: parasitic-extraction-spef
outputs.desc: SPEF files for each extraction corner

outputs.name: timing-signoff-report
outputs.desc: Setup and hold slack at all corners with worst negative slack and total negative slack

process: Parasitic extraction: the extraction tool reads the GDSII layout and the process technology file (ITF/QRC tech file). It builds an RC network model for each net: resistance from wire length, width, and sheet resistance; capacitance from wire-to-wire coupling and wire-to-ground. Output is SPEF (Standard Parasitic Exchange Format).

Extract at multiple RC corners: typical (Ctyp), minimum (Cmin: best-case capacitance, worst for hold), maximum (Cmax: worst-case capacitance, worst for setup). The RC corners capture manufacturing variation in metal thickness and dielectric properties.

Static timing analysis (STA): read the gate-level netlist, SDC constraints, cell library timing models (.lib), and SPEF. The STA tool computes arrival times and required times at every pin in the design. Slack = required_time - arrival_time (positive is good).

Multi-corner multi-mode (MCMM) signoff: run STA at all PVT corners simultaneously. Setup check: slow process, high temperature, Cmax, low voltage. Hold check: fast process, low temperature, Cmin, high voltage. Apply OCV derating to launch and capture paths.

CRPR (Clock Reconvergence Pessimism Removal): when the launch and capture clocks share common tree segments, OCV is applied to both, creating artificial pessimism. CRPR removes the extra derating on the shared portion. Always enable CRPR for signoff to avoid over-design.

Signoff criteria: zero negative slack on setup and hold at all signoff corners. Report worst negative slack (WNS) and total negative slack (TNS). If violations remain, fix with ECO (engineering change order): resize cells, insert buffers, swap cells to different Vt flavors, or reroute critical nets. Re-extract and re-time after each ECO.

description: Design the test infrastructure for an IC including scan chains, ATPG, memory BIST, JTAG boundary scan, and test compression to achieve target fault coverage at acceptable test cost.

steps.description: Insert scan chains into the design, converting flip-flops to scan flip-flops and partitioning into chains for controllability and observability during manufacturing test.

inputs.name: gate-level-netlist
inputs.desc: Synthesized netlist with flip-flop instances

inputs.name: test-requirements
inputs.desc: Fault coverage target, number of scan chains, test clock frequency

outputs.name: scan-inserted-netlist
outputs.desc: Netlist with scan flip-flops connected into chains

outputs.name: scan-chain-report
outputs.desc: Number of chains, chain lengths, scan-in/scan-out pin assignments

process: Replace all non-scan flip-flops with scan equivalents: the scan flip-flop adds a multiplexer at the data input, selecting between functional data (in normal mode) and scan-in data (in test mode). Area overhead is approximately 10-15% for the mux addition.

Determine the number of scan chains: more chains means shorter shift time (parallel loading) but more I/O pins. If pins are limited, use test compression (handled in a later step) to reduce the number of physical scan-in/scan-out pins. Typical: 4-32 physical chains without compression, 200-2000 internal chains with compression.

Chain balancing: distribute flip-flops evenly across chains so all chains have approximately the same length. Unbalanced chains waste shift cycles (the longest chain determines the shift count). Also consider physical proximity: chain flip-flops near each other to minimize routing congestion of the scan chain wiring.

Handle special flip-flops: clock gating cells (ICGs) need special scan treatment (test mode bypasses the gate). Multi-bit flip-flops are stitched as a group. Reset flip-flops need their reset controlled during scan mode to prevent corruption.

Lockup latches: if a scan chain crosses clock domains or has timing issues between stages (the scan shift path does not meet hold timing), insert lockup latches (transparent latches) at the domain boundary to prevent race conditions during shift.

Verify scan connectivity: run a scan chain trace to confirm all flip-flops are in chains, no flip-flops are missing, and the chains shift correctly (shift-in a known pattern, shift-out and compare). This is done in simulation before ATPG.

steps.description: Generate automatic test patterns to detect stuck-at, transition, and bridging faults, measuring fault coverage and diagnosing untestable faults.

inputs.name: scan-inserted-netlist
inputs.desc: Scan-inserted design

inputs.name: test-requirements
inputs.desc: Target fault coverage (typically 95-99%)

outputs.name: test-patterns
outputs.desc: ATPG pattern set in STIL or WGL format

outputs.name: fault-coverage-report
outputs.desc: Fault coverage breakdown: detected, possibly detected, untestable, not detected

process: Stuck-at fault model: each net is assumed stuck at 0 or stuck at 1. For N nets, there are 2N faults. ATPG generates patterns that sensitize each fault (create a condition where the faulty value propagates to an observable output). Target: >98% stuck-at coverage.

Transition (delay) fault model: each net has a slow-to-rise and slow-to-fall fault. The pattern must launch a transition at the fault site and capture the result one clock cycle later at-speed. Two launch methods: launch-off-shift (last shift clock launches the transition, capture clock captures) and launch-off-capture (a functional clock edge launches, next edge captures).

Launch-off-capture is preferred for delay testing because it exercises functional timing paths. Launch-off-shift may create false paths (the shift data does not represent a functional state). However, launch-off-capture requires two-cycle patterns and may have lower coverage for combinational paths.

Run ATPG: the tool generates patterns, reports fault coverage, and classifies undetected faults. Untestable faults include: redundant logic (the fault cannot be observed because the logic is redundant by design), blocked faults (no path to an observable point), and faults on test-mode-only logic.

For undetected non-untestable faults: analyze why ATPG could not find a pattern. Common causes: insufficient controllability (add test points: control points inject values, observe points add output paths), incomplete scan (some flip-flops not in scan), or ATPG tool limits (increase effort level).

Pattern count vs test time: each pattern requires shifting all scan chains (shift_count = chain_length cycles) plus one or two capture cycles. Total test time = N_patterns * (shift_count + capture_cycles) / test_clock_frequency. If test time exceeds the ATE budget, reduce patterns (accept slightly lower coverage) or use compression.

steps.description: Design built-in self-test for embedded memories using March algorithms, with repair analysis for redundancy allocation.

inputs.name: memory-instances
inputs.desc: List of embedded SRAMs/ROMs with sizes, types, and locations

inputs.name: test-requirements
inputs.desc: Memory fault coverage targets and test time constraints

outputs.name: bist-controller-design
outputs.desc: MBIST controller with selected March algorithm and configuration

outputs.name: repair-analysis
outputs.desc: Redundancy allocation (spare rows/columns) and expected repair yield improvement

process: Embedded SRAM faults: stuck-at faults in cells, address decoder faults, coupling faults between adjacent cells (a write to cell A flips cell B), transition faults (cell cannot transition from 0 to 1 or vice versa), and data retention faults.

March algorithm selection: March C- detects all stuck-at and transition faults with 10N operations (where N is the number of cells). March SS adds coupling fault detection with 22N operations. For most production testing, March C- is sufficient. March algorithms apply a sequence of read/write operations in ascending and descending address order.

MBIST controller design: the controller generates the address sequence, data patterns (all-0, all-1, checkerboard, inverse checkerboard), and the march element sequence. It compares read data against expected data and flags failures with the failing address and data bit. One controller can test multiple memories by multiplexing.

For large SoCs with hundreds of memory instances: use a hierarchical BIST architecture. A top-level controller manages multiple local BIST controllers. Memories are grouped by type and size for efficient testing. Test scheduling runs independent memories in parallel to reduce total test time.

Redundancy and repair: SRAM compilers include spare rows and spare columns. If a cell fails, the row or column containing it is replaced by the spare. The MBIST controller logs failing addresses, and a repair analysis algorithm determines the optimal spare allocation. Typical repair: 1-4 spare rows and 1-4 spare columns per memory block.

Calculate the yield improvement from redundancy: without repair, yield = (1 - p_fail)^N_cells. With repair, yield improves by the probability that all failures can be covered by the available spares. For a 256KB SRAM with 4 spare rows and 4 spare columns, yield improvement is typically 5-15% absolute.

steps.description: Implement test compression (LBIST or codec-based) to reduce scan test data volume and test time while maintaining fault coverage.

inputs.name: scan-inserted-netlist
inputs.desc: Design with internal scan chains

inputs.name: test-patterns
inputs.desc: Uncompressed ATPG patterns with pattern count and data volume

outputs.name: compressed-test-architecture
outputs.desc: Decompressor and compactor design with compression ratio

outputs.name: compressed-patterns
outputs.desc: Compressed test patterns with updated fault coverage

process: Without compression: for 1000 internal scan chains of 500 flip-flops each, test data volume = 1000 * 500 * N_patterns bits. At 500 MHz ATE speed with 32 physical channels, test time = data_volume / (32 * 500M). For 5000 patterns, this is approximately 80 seconds per die, costing approximately $0.10/die on modern ATE.

Codec-based compression (e.g., Synopsys DFTMAX, Cadence Modus): a decompressor expands a small number of physical scan-in channels to many internal chains. The decompressor uses a linear-feedback shift register (LFSR) seeded by the ATE data to generate the internal chain inputs. Only the specified (care) bits need to match; do not care bits are filled by the LFSR.

Compression ratio: typical ATPG patterns have 1-5% specified (care) bits. A 100:1 compression ratio is achievable, mapping 32 physical channels to 3200 internal chains. This reduces test time by 100x. The compactor on the output side XOR-combines multiple chain outputs into fewer physical scan-out channels.

Compression vs coverage trade-off: higher compression may reduce fault coverage because the decompressor cannot set all arbitrary care-bit combinations (aliasing). Typically, coverage drop is < 0.5% for 100:1 compression. If coverage drops below target, reduce the compression ratio or add dedicated test points.

LBIST (Logic BIST): the LFSR generates pseudo-random patterns applied to the scan chains. No external ATE data needed during test. Coverage is limited by random-pattern-resistant faults (faults requiring specific input combinations that pseudo-random patterns rarely generate). Typical stuck-at coverage from LBIST: 85-95%. Supplement with stored test points or weighted random patterns to improve.

Hybrid approach: use LBIST for initial high-coverage testing (fast, low cost), then apply a small set of compressed deterministic patterns for the remaining hard-to-detect faults. This minimizes total test cost while achieving >99% fault coverage.

steps.description: Analyze manufacturing test results to identify systematic defects, correlate failures to process excursions, and feed learnings back to design and process for yield improvement.

inputs.name: test-results
inputs.desc: Pass/fail data, failing patterns, and failing scan chains from production testing

inputs.name: wafer-map-data
inputs.desc: Pass/fail by die position on the wafer

outputs.name: defect-analysis
outputs.desc: Identified systematic defect types, locations, and root causes

outputs.name: yield-improvement-actions
outputs.desc: Design or process changes to eliminate identified defects

process: Wafer map analysis: plot pass/fail by die position. Random defects scatter uniformly. Systematic defects form spatial patterns: edge failures (lithography or CMP edge effects), cluster defects (particle contamination), ring patterns (spin-on process), or quadrant patterns (reticle defects).

Shmoo plotting: vary test conditions (voltage, frequency, temperature) and map the pass/fail boundary. The shmoo plot reveals how much margin the design has. A design that fails at the nominal corner but passes at relaxed conditions indicates a borderline timing or noise margin issue.

Fail bitmap analysis for memories: map failing bit addresses to physical locations on the memory array. Random single-bit failures indicate particle defects. Row or column failures indicate decoder or word-line/bit-line defects. Adjacent-cell failures indicate coupling or lithography issues.

Scan diagnosis: from the failing test pattern and the failing scan chain output, the diagnosis tool traces back through the circuit to identify candidate defect locations. It narrows down to a small region of the layout where the defect likely resides. Physical failure analysis (SEM, FIB cross-section) at that location confirms the defect.

Volume diagnosis: aggregate diagnosis results from thousands of failing dies. The most frequently diagnosed defect locations indicate systematic design weaknesses (layout sensitivities, marginal timing paths). These are candidates for targeted design fixes (ECO).

Feedback loop: provide the defect data to the process team (for process excursion control) and to the design team (for design rule improvement or circuit redesign). Track yield over time: a rising yield curve confirms that corrective actions are working. A sudden yield drop triggers immediate investigation for new defect sources.
